title: The Part of Stacy Sims You Don't See
description: Team, I want to tell you something about Dr. Stacy Sims that has nothing to do with fasting, or protein, or any of the science that made her name. You know her as the woman who proved that women are not small men. The TED talk. The books. The movement. The scientist who spent twenty years forcing women back into research that had erased them. What you do not see is what it cost her to become that person. In our conversation, Stacy told me something she said she has never shared on a podcast before. There was a time she tried to take her own life, and was hospitalized afterward. She has carried that quietly for years, underneath the global brand and the stage lights and the certainty you see on camera. It took real courage to say it out loud, and she said it to help any woman listening who is sitting in the same dark place she once was. And even now, she is still a target. For the simple act of saying that women deserve their own science, she gets attacked online every single day, by people who have never met her, never had one conversation with her, running off a clickbait clip. She told me it left her with PTSD. The worst of it came when her own daughter picked up a phone, saw a stranger’s cruelty aimed at her mother, and asked whether it was safe to go outside. Sit with that for a second. A woman who has given her entire career to helping other women get stronger and live longer, watching her child become frightened because of what people type. And she keeps going. She keeps publishing, keeps standing on stages, keeps saying the thing the data says even when going quiet would be so much easier. Not because she enjoys the fight, but because she decided a long time ago that someone had to carry this, and it would be her. That is the woman behind the science.

title: This Is Why You Wake Up at 3am
description: We have a new podcast studio!!! Team, you all know that I have been doing my podcast since 2016 - holy moly, it’s been 10 years!!!!!!! I have gone from recording audio only to recording on a $30 microphone in my first New York City apartment. I have gone all over the world to interview guests, and now I have my very own beautiful white studio! Go watch this one. I mean it. I sat down with Dr. Michael Breus, the Sleep Doctor, and I left rethinking things I was sure I already understood. He has spent his whole career as a clinical psychologist doing one thing, fixing the way people sleep, and he is blunt in a way I loved. First thing that floored me: the Sleep Doctor himself stops breathing 26 times an hour in his sleep, and had no idea for years. How he found out: His workouts were falling apart and his mile time kept climbing He ran bloodwork, even tried testosterone, chasing every other explanation first Nothing moved Finally someone asked when he’d last done a sleep study It came back 26. He was so sure it was broken that he retook it. Same number. The Sleep Doctor had sleep apnea and didn’t know. Here’s why that should scare the rest of us: It can happen anywhere from 5 to hundreds of times an hour, and most people never know it’s happening Every time you stop breathing, your heart rate drops then spikes to restart you, loading your heart all night long. Over time that can tip into atrial fibrillation. You’re also starving your brain of oxygen, and you never sink into the deep sleep where the brain runs its own cleanup His tell for spotting it across a room: a neck over 17.5 inches carries an 83 percent chance of apnea (his number) And one story I won’t forget: a detective, benched because he kept falling asleep on stakeouts, finally got on a CPAP.
